# The SGLang configuration space

The compute stack map, applied to one piece of software and only to its settings:
every flag of an SGLang server and its gateway and every env var, laid on the
inference stack from platform to fleet, with every place the code lets one setting
depend on another.

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `config_space.html` | The page. Four views: the map, the coupling graph, what moves what, and how dense it is. Generated. Published at https://claude.ai/artifact/M4TW6n2Biq8jSLHTghJYsy |
| `ontology/` | Judgement: layers, groups, which flags belong where, and curated notes on the knobs people tune. |
| `data/catalog.json` | Facts: flags, env vars, rules and model overrides, extracted from the SGLang source. Generated. |
| `data/config_space.json` | The two joined and validated, with the coupling graph computed. Generated. |

## Building

    python3 src/extract.py ../sglang     # refresh the catalog from a checkout, when the code moves
    python3 src/build.py                 # validate, compute couplings, write config_space.html

`extract.py` reads the source statically, so nothing of SGLang has to be importable:

    flags       python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/*.py  (A[type, help] annotations, Arg(...) metadata,
                the section banner each field sits under) plus the few flags server_args.py adds by hand
    gateway     sgl-model-gateway/src/main.rs, struct CliArgs (clap attributes and doc comments)
    envs        python/sglang/srt/environ.py, class Envs (default, type, section, the comment above)
    rules       every raise/assert whose condition names flags (a refusal), and every flag written
                from a value computed from other flags (a default change), across arg_groups/,
                the model overrides and server_args.py. Local variables carry the flags they were
                computed from; small helper predicates are followed one level.
    overrides   @_register_for(...) hooks in arg_groups/model_overrides/: architecture -> flags it sets

`resolve.py` (run by `build.py`) refuses to write anything unless every flag and every
env-var section lands in exactly one group, and every curated knob, metric and objective
reference resolves.

## The ontology

    ontology/ontology.yaml     schema: kinds, id scheme, vocabularies, relations, palette
    ontology/metrics.yaml      metrics, objectives, and contexts (the GPU, the model, the workload)
    ontology/l1_platform.yaml  one file per layer, bottom of the stack to the top
    ontology/l2_model.yaml
    ontology/l3_kernels.yaml
    ontology/l4_execution.yaml
    ontology/l5_memory.yaml
    ontology/l6_scheduling.yaml
    ontology/l7_serving.yaml

Ids read `<layer>.<group>.<knob>`, for example `l5.radix.radix-eviction-policy`; gateway
flags carry a `gw-` prefix, env vars are `env.<NAME>`. Ids are permanent, and the page
deep-links to them: `config_space.html#l5.pool.page-size`.

A group claims flags two ways. `select` takes every flag in a namespace and code section;
`take` names flags explicitly and wins over any selector, which is how a flag filed
under the wrong section in the code ends up in the right box here. `envs` claims whole
env-var sections. `moves` is the default set of metrics for the group's knobs.

A knob is curated only where it is worth it: `tier` (primary, advanced, niche),
`summary`, `moves`, `breaks` (how it goes wrong in practice) and `typical`. Everything
else the page shows about a knob (type, default, choices, help, source line, couplings)
comes from the catalog and is never written by hand. Uncurated knobs default to `niche`
and are described by the first sentence of their own help text.

## What the numbers mean

A coupling is two flags named in the same rule. It is a lower bound: checks that fire
later, inside kernels or model code, are not seen, and the gateway's Rust code is not
scanned for rules. It can over-link where a large function computes many values from one
condition. The GPU and the model are not flags, but a rule that branches on them is
marked, and the page counts them separately.

At sgl-project/sglang@b252aceffe: 515 server flags, 93 gateway flags, 648 env vars,
954 rules (491 refusals, 463 default changes). 218 server flags appear in no rule; 258 are
coupled, 232 of them in one connected cluster, and 105 are each tied to five or more
others.

# Inference optimization techniques

Every inference optimization technique described by three sources, laid on the inference
stack from the workload down to the silicon, with a write-up, canonical examples and the
effect sizes each source reports, all linked to the page they came from.

Sources:

- [Doubleword blog](https://blog.doubleword.ai/): all 63 posts.
- [wafer-ai/gpu-perf-engineering-resources](https://github.com/wafer-ai/gpu-perf-engineering-resources):
  every resource the README links, about 120 papers, posts, docs and repos.
- [Inferact: 700 TPS on Kimi K3, a case for TPU megakernels](https://inferact.ai/blog/tpu-megakernels),
  and the repository it releases.

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `inference_optimizations.html` | The page: map, full write-ups, effect sizes, sources, unmapped. Generated. Published at https://claude.ai/artifact/Ppy99C282sgbCktwTkivwr |
| `ontology/taxonomy.yaml` | Bands of the stack, kinds of technique, the three sources. |
| `ontology/techniques/*.yaml` | The curated techniques, one file per curation job. |
| `research/*.yaml` | Raw records from the research pass, one file per batch of sources. |
| `research/SCHEMA.md`, `research/CURATION.md` | The formats and rules both passes followed. |

## How it was made

1. **Research**, nine parallel batches: four for the Doubleword posts (16 each), four for the
   sections of the wafer-ai list (every linked resource opened), one for the Inferact post
   and its repo. Each wrote one record per technique found (`research/SCHEMA.md`): level, kind,
   parent, a write-up, examples, effect sizes with the exact page and section, sources.
   Pages were read with `src/fetch_text.py`, which keeps numbers and heading anchors.
2. **Grouping**: `src/merge.py` groups records that share a name or alias across batches;
   `src/jobs.py` splits the groups into ten curation jobs and gives each a permanent id.
3. **Curation**, ten parallel jobs (`research/CURATION.md`): fix the grouping, write one
   consolidated record per technique, keep every example, effect size and source, and
   account for every raw record in `merged_from`.
4. **Build**: `src/build.py` folds cross-job duplicates, checks that every raw record landed
   in exactly one technique, that parents exist and are high-level, and that every effect
   size has a source URL, then writes the page.

    python3 src/merge.py && python3 src/jobs.py    # only when research/ changes
    python3 src/build.py

## Reading the numbers

Effect sizes are what each source reports, under the conditions it states, never re-measured.
`multiplier_low`/`multiplier_high` convert a claim to an improvement factor where one comparison
allows it (30% faster = 1.3x; 40% less memory = 1.67x). Claims that compare different setups
keep their text but carry no factor. Numbers from different models, chips and baselines are
not comparable across techniques; compare within a row.

## Levels and kinds

A **high-level** technique is a strategy you would name in a design review (speculative
decoding, KV cache offloading, tensor parallelism). A **low-level** technique is a mechanism
that implements one (tree attention for verification, TMA async copies, rANS entropy coding)
and names its parent. Kinds and bands are defined in `ontology/taxonomy.yaml`. Anything that
fits no kind is kept on the **unmapped** list with a reason, never dropped.
